intro: Paderewski’s 1917 Nocturne documents an older approach to melodic freedom. Jonathan Woolf describes his recorded playing in terms of hand dislocation, arpeggiated chords and flexible rhythm: the hands need not attack together for the phrase to remain coherent. Listen for that possibility without treating every sound on a historic transfer as a deliberate interpretive choice.
question: Does separating melody and accompaniment change which note you hear as the beginning of a phrase?

sections.label: A′ · Larghetto returns
sections.mNote: the opening song returns after the faster middle

cues.title: Listen between the hands
cues.text: Paderewski’s recorded style includes attacks that separate the melody from its accompaniment. Listen for whether the upper note arrives with the supporting chord or seems to speak independently of it.
cues.evidence: Jonathan Woolf discusses constant desynchronisation/dislocation and arpeggiation in the Victor recordings, including this Nocturne: https://www.musicweb-international.com/classrev/2017/May/Paderewski_American_7505.htm . This establishes a stylistic practice, not a measured delay at this timestamp.

cues.title: The 1917 master
cues.text: This recording was made in New York on 14 May 1917. DAHR identifies the issued master as take 1 of matrix C-19781, linking both Victor 74529 and the Gramophone issues used by this transfer to the same performance.

cues.title: Freedom has more than one kind
cues.text: Separating the hands is not the same as slowing both together. A melody can seem to linger against its accompaniment; a whole phrase can also expand or contract. Keep those two kinds of timing distinct while listening.
cues.evidence: Explanation of dislocation versus phrase-level rubato, grounded in Woolf’s description: https://www.musicweb-international.com/classrev/2017/May/Paderewski_American_7505.htm. No particular delay is timed.

cues.title: Paderewski on rubato
cues.text: In his 1909 essay on tempo rubato, Paderewski rejects a mechanical rule that every stolen moment must be repaid immediately. His argument concerns expressive freedom within a phrase, not permission to ignore all rhythmic relations.
cues.evidence: Paderewski’s essay in Henry T. Finck, Success in Music, reproduced by USC Polish Music Center: https://polishmusic.usc.edu/research/publications/polish-music-journal/vol4no1/paderewski-tempo-rubato/

cues.title: The faster central span
cues.text: The score’s doppio movimento replaces the slower opening movement with a more active middle. Listen for the difference between Chopin’s written change of pace and the smaller timing adjustments a performer makes within it.
cues.evidence: Approximate middle around1:36, before the central crest at2:00–2:10. Report novelty near1:36 supports a passage-level marker; score headings: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A retreat before recognition
cues.text: The central force withdraws before the slower song returns. Listen for the space left by the accompaniment as well as the melody: balance between the hands helps determine how a returning phrase speaks.
cues.evidence: Report level decreases sharply between the central crest around 2:00 and the low window at 2:25. No particular pedalling, voicing or note delay is inferred from the waveform.

cues.title: The opening becomes familiar again
cues.text: The slower opening material returns. Comparing this reprise with the first statement is a better test of Paderewski’s timing than imposing a single metronome speed on the whole recording.
cues.evidence: Estimated reprise around2:24 after the central retreat. Reprise form: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173. Timing is approximate and does not depend on comparing this transfer’s total duration with a different transfer.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The transfer is not the session
cues.text: The original disc and its modern digital copy have different histories. The Public Domain Project identifies the HMV carrier and its collection source, but does not establish every transfer decision. Noise, speed or equalisation should not be attributed automatically to Paderewski.
cues.evidence: Upstream carrier/transfer record: https://pool.musicalheritage.org/index.php?title=Hmv-db375-05616 . Session attribution independently confirmed by DAHR; undocumented processing remains unknown.

transitions.title: The written tempo contrast changes the texture
transitions.how: The opening song yields to the faster middle marked doppio movimento. This structural change is distinct from Paderewski’s smaller expressive timing adjustments. Faster activity and a more concentrated texture establish a new span, which then gathers dynamic force rather than beginning at its maximum intensity.
transitions.evidence: Approximate boundary near the1:36 novelty peak; the report’s central crest occurs around2:00–2:10. Markings and form: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173

transitions.title: The middle clears space for the song
transitions.how: The middle’s dynamic and rhythmic pressure relaxes, allowing the slower song and its ornamented line to return. The reprise recalls a familiar relationship between melody and accompaniment. Listen for whether the melodic attack coincides with its support or seems to speak just before or after it.
transitions.evidence: Approximate placement around 2:24 after a marked fall in level at 2:15–2:25; score reprise: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/173 . The section marker does not measure hand dislocation; the listening invitation is grounded in Woolf’s documented stylistic account.

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
